title: Predictive causal control of microbiome–immune interactions

concept.text: The proposed innovation is the ability to predict and deliberately change immune responses by controlling defined microbial products and the host pathways through which they act. It would connect a microbial molecule or activity to a specific immune mechanism, establish that changing it causes an immune effect, and predict the outcome of a targeted intervention in a new person or setting. The intended capability extends beyond identifying microbial patterns associated with health or disease.

A concrete example motivating this direction is food-allergy research connecting fecal microbiome transplantation, regulatory T cells, bile acid metabolites and oral tolerance. The supplied review describes preliminary human responses alongside experiments transferring responder microbiomes into mice. This example provides a starting point for investigating causal mechanisms; it does not demonstrate the proposed general ability to predict and control microbiome-driven immune responses.

As a synthesis of the intended scope, a useful system would explain when a microbial intervention changes immune tolerance or inflammation, why its effects differ between settings, and where its predictions cease to apply. Differences among people, tissues, diets and time are candidate sources of context dependence to investigate. The supplied evidence does not establish their respective contributions or document the field-wide extent of the remaining capability gap.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability could turn microbiome research into a basis for mechanistically targeted immune intervention. Instead of selecting an intervention primarily because a microbial community correlates with an outcome, researchers could select a defined microbial product or function because its causal pathway and expected immune effects were understood. The food-allergy example gives this possibility a concrete biological basis through its reported links among transplantation, immune-tolerance cells and metabolites.

Conditional downstream possibilities include selecting interventions for particular patients, replacing some complex community transfers with defined products, and predicting circumstances in which an intervention would fail or cause an unwanted immune effect. These are proposed consequences of successful causal prediction, not demonstrated applications in the supplied evidence. Their feasibility would depend on whether defined products reproduce the relevant community functions and can be controlled in the host.

The impact would remain bounded by intervention-specific evidence. Predicting an immune marker would not by itself establish disease prevention or treatment, and an effect in food allergy would not establish comparable control of autoimmunity, cancer or systemic inflammation. Nor would this breakthrough by itself close the missing-heritability gap: explaining microbial contributions to immune outcomes is distinct from accounting for unexplained inherited variation. No such heritability result is established here.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability sought by this proposal is a transferable causal account linking microbial products, host immune pathways and intervention outcomes. The supplied material documents one relevant food-allergy example, but does not establish how broadly this capability remains absent across immunology as of 1 November 2026. The broader gap should therefore be understood as the innovation's research target, with its present field-wide extent unresolved.

A concrete scientific barrier is separating the effects of individual microbial products from the many changes introduced by a community transplant. In the reviewed example, responder-microbiome transfers protected mice, regulatory T-cell changes were reported in human responders, and bile acid metabolites increased in humans and mice. These observations motivate mechanistic investigation, but the supplied preview does not establish that a particular bile acid is necessary and sufficient for the human response or that a particular host pathway mediates that response. A community-transfer result and a metabolite association answer different causal questions.

As an engineering synthesis, achieving the proposed capability would require reproducible measurement of relevant microbial activities and products, interventions that alter them predictably, and evidence connecting exposure to the intended host pathway. Researchers would also need to determine how host state and environmental context change these relationships. A useful predictor must retain accuracy when tested prospectively outside the population and conditions used to develop it, with clear limits where transfer fails.

Clinical control adds a further barrier: the intended immune effect must produce a meaningful benefit with acceptable safety and sufficient durability. Mechanistic animal experiments can help isolate causal steps, but their results cannot substitute for controlled human evidence. Likewise, identifying an associated immune-cell change does not establish that manipulating that cell population will reproduce the clinical effect.

current_state.text: According to the supplied review, Katrina Ray's research highlight, published on 20 August 2026, describes Rachid et al.'s 2026 study, “Fecal microbiome transplant in food allergy in humans and mice identifies a role for bile acid metabolites in oral tolerance.” The highlight reports an open-label phase I trial involving 15 participants with peanut allergy who received encapsulated fecal microbiome transplantation. Six participants showed an increased peanut-reactivity threshold. This is a preliminary human response observation; the open-label study does not establish controlled efficacy, a cure or a general human treatment.

The highlight also reports an increase in tolerogenic RORγt-positive regulatory T cells in responders, protection against the development of food allergy in mice receiving responder microbiomes, and increased bile acid metabolites in humans and mice. Together, these findings connect a human intervention with immune observations and mechanistic animal experiments. The mouse protection concerns development of food allergy and should not be recast as demonstrated reversal of established human allergy. The metabolite findings remain mechanistic leads rather than proof of a defined metabolite treatment in people.

Access limits affect how precisely these findings can be described. The supplied review identifies the Nature material as a subscription preview. The retained PubMed artifact contains a cookie-access message rather than an identifiable article abstract, so it cannot verify the primary paper's scientific details. In particular, participant adulthood, the previously asserted primary publication date of 5 August 2026, and the asserted DOI 10.1126/scitranslmed.aee3263 remain unverified from the retained texts. The earlier assertion that primary abstract text was available is not substantiated by those materials. These limitations do not negate the narrower findings reported in the Nature preview.

The supplied evidence establishes a dated example, not a comprehensive account of the field. The review reports an empty bounded search record, leaving coverage through 1 November 2026 unresolved. It therefore cannot establish whether later or additional work has demonstrated broader predictive control. That uncertainty is separate from the interpretation of the August 2026 findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: identify defined microbial products and the host immune pathways through which they act, then perturb both sides of the proposed causal relationship in suitable mechanistic models and human studies. Where feasible, removing or blocking the proposed mediator should weaken the effect, and restoring it should recover the effect. Such experiments would help distinguish a causal microbial product from a correlated marker and identify whether a host pathway is required. These are proposed evidentiary tests, not established consensus requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Perturbing microbial products and host pathways establishes immune causality

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration of predictive breadth: make prospective predictions of immune outcomes in independent populations and test the approach across more than one tissue or immune condition. Predictions should specify the intervention, outcome, measurement period and expected uncertainty before results are known. Success would establish the breadth actually tested; finite demonstrations would not establish literal universality across people, tissues or diseases.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective predictions generalize across independent populations and multiple immune contexts

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration of clinical usefulness: show in controlled human trials that a targeted intervention changes a clinically meaningful outcome, rather than only a microbial measurement, metabolite concentration or immune-cell marker. Independent reproduction should confirm the relevant mechanism and benefit. Practical evaluation should address consistency of intervention composition and exposure, durability, adverse effects, and the patient groups and contexts in which the intervention works. The supplied evidence does not justify prescribing numerical success thresholds or a universal trial design.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled human trials demonstrate independently reproduced clinical benefit

completion_criteria.text: These proposed criteria deliberately extend beyond the documented food-allergy example. Its combination of human intervention and responder-microbiome experiments in mice illustrates a useful bridge between clinical observation and mechanistic testing, while leaving prospective generalization and controlled human benefit to be demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Food-allergy evidence leaves prospective generalization and controlled human benefit unproven

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: IMM-02, “A predictive, causal theory of whole immune responses,” is the broadest overlap. IMM-13 addresses microbial inputs and their host pathways, whereas IMM-02 seeks prediction across the wider immune system. IMM-01, “A general decoder for T-cell antigen recognition,” concerns recognition of antigens by T cells; that could inform some microbial effects, but it does not encompass all metabolite-mediated or other microbiome–immune interactions.

IMM-11, “Causal mechanisms that initiate the breakdown of self-tolerance,” overlaps where microbial signals contribute to loss of tolerance. IMM-04, “Durable, antigen-specific reversal of established autoimmunity,” and IMM-05, “Routine donor-specific transplant tolerance without lifelong immunosuppression,” concern particular therapeutic forms of tolerance. Predictive microbiome control could contribute to these goals, but food-allergy oral tolerance, reversal of established autoimmunity and donor-specific graft acceptance are distinct outcomes requiring separate evidence.

IMM-12, “Programmable trained immunity with predictable protection and safety,” overlaps if microbial products produce lasting changes in innate immune responsiveness. That differs from the regulatory T-cell and oral-tolerance mechanisms highlighted here. IMM-03, “Vaccine design that reliably directs broadly protective antibody evolution,” concerns directing antibody development; microbial modulation could affect its context without establishing control over antibody evolution.

IMM-10, “Real-time immune control of life-threatening systemic inflammation,” shares the aim of controlling inflammatory responses, but adds acute timing and physiological control requirements beyond this concept. IMM-14, “Causal, bidirectional control of neuroimmune circuits,” shares a causal-control ambition while focusing on signaling between nervous and immune systems. Microbial influences might intersect with those circuits, but the supplied food-allergy evidence does not establish that connection.

IMM-06, “General immune eradication of heterogeneous solid tumors,” IMM-07, “Immune-mediated, treatment-free control of established HIV infection,” and IMM-08, “Restoration of youthful immune competence in older adults,” identify separate disease or functional endpoints. Microbiome interventions could conceivably contribute to them, but none follows from demonstrated changes in food-allergy responses. IMM-09, “In-body programming of immune cells as an inexpensive, scalable treatment,” concerns a delivery and programming capability; IMM-13 instead concerns predicting and controlling microbial influences, regardless of the eventual intervention platform.

unresolved_issues: The primary paper's participant age range, exact publication date, DOI and full scientific details remain unverified from the retained texts.
The Nature subscription preview does not provide enough information here to assess response magnitude, response duration, adverse events or the complete experimental design.
The supplied evidence does not establish whether particular bile acid metabolites are necessary or sufficient for the human response, or which host pathways causally mediate it.
Coverage through 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied bounded search record is empty; the field-wide extent of the remaining predictive-control gap cannot be determined.
The appropriate numerical targets for predictive accuracy, durability, clinical benefit and safety remain to be defined for specific interventions and indications.

brief.title: Predicting and steering immunity through gut microbes
possible: People could receive treatments chosen to change a specific immune response through the microbes in their gut. Researchers could predict how a defined microbial product would act in a new person, then deliberately change it to influence tolerance or inflammation.

Doctors could select treatments for particular patients and anticipate when they might fail or cause unwanted immune effects. Defined microbial products could replace some transfers of whole microbial communities.
why: Researchers could choose treatments because they understand how a microbial product causes an immune effect. That would give them a clearer basis for treatment than an association between certain microbes and health.

For people with food allergies, this could provide a route to treatments that help the immune system tolerate food. Understanding the mechanism would also help explain why responses differ between people.

sources.showed: Their food-allergy study combined a preliminary human trial of capsules containing transferred gut microbes with mouse experiments. Some participants tolerated more peanut before reacting, and mice receiving responding participants’ microbes resisted developing food allergy.
sources.cited_for: The study connects a human intervention with experiments testing the effects of transferred microbial communities in mice.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a defined microbial product that predictably treats food allergy in people.

sources.showed: Ray describes Rachid and colleagues’ study. Six participants needed more peanut to trigger a reaction after treatment, and mice receiving responding participants’ gut microbial communities were protected against developing food allergy.
sources.quote: mice transplanted with the microbiomes of responders were protected from the development of food allergy
sources.cited_for: The research highlight reports preliminary human responses alongside protective effects in mice.
sources.not_established: The human trial lacked a comparison group, so it does not establish treatment benefit or prediction across different settings.

shown: Rima Rachid and colleagues linked a human food-allergy intervention to protective effects in mice. Their small trial gave people with peanut allergy capsules containing transferred gut microbes. Some could then tolerate more peanut before reacting.

Responding participants also had more regulatory T cells, immune cells that help restrain immune reactions. Their gut microbes protected mice against developing food allergy. The human trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew the treatment being given.
missing: A defined microbial product must be shown to cause the human immune response through a specific pathway in the body.
Predictions must hold when tested in new populations and different immune conditions.
Controlled human trials must demonstrate meaningful, lasting benefit with acceptable safety, confirmed by independent teams.

milestones.label: Changing microbial products and immune pathways proves cause and effect
milestones.explanation: Changing a defined microbial product and the body’s proposed response pathway would have to alter the immune effect as predicted. This would distinguish a cause from a marker that merely accompanies the response.

milestones.label: Predictions succeed in new populations and different immune settings
milestones.explanation: Predictions made before outcomes are known would have to succeed in independent populations and across different tissues or immune conditions. This would establish how widely the approach applies.

milestones.label: Independent controlled trials confirm clinical benefit
milestones.explanation: Controlled human trials would have to show meaningful health benefits, with independent teams reproducing the mechanism and benefit. This would establish usefulness beyond changes in microbes or immune measurements.

milestones.label: Food-allergy findings leave prediction and controlled benefit unresolved
milestones.explanation: Food-allergy research would still have to demonstrate predictions in new settings and controlled human benefit. This would carry its link between human observations and mouse experiments toward the broader capability.

uncertain: Which microbial products are required for the human response, and can those products reproduce it on their own?
How much do differences in people, tissues, diets and time change an intervention’s effects?
What levels of predictive accuracy, lasting benefit and safety would count as success for each treatment?

page.title: Predictive control of microbiome–immune interactions
page.definition: A model predicts how changing a specified product or activity of the gut microbiome—the resident microbial community—changes a human immune response. Interventions reproduce those predictions through an experimentally established host pathway in people outside the development cohort.

goal.need: An open-label peanut-allergy study reported responses in 6 of 15 adults receiving transferred gut microbes. Deleting a microbial bile-salt-hydrolase gene abolished protection in mice, providing a mechanistic lead. NIH identifies microbiome effects on disease and treatment response as research targets. The remaining task is to connect a defined mechanism to a prospectively predicted human response.

figures.caption: Responses in the phase I peanut-allergy microbiome-transplant study
figures.note: Response meant an increased peanut reactivity threshold. These small, open-label groups do not establish an antibiotic treatment effect.

statements.body: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
statements.quote: Projects should focus on evaluating how to alter the microbiome to treat and prevent disease, understand how the microbiome affects treatment response
statements.context: The NIH topic includes allergies, inflammatory bowel disease and other immune-mediated diseases.

statements.body: White House Office of Science and Technology Policy
statements.quote: Understanding these principles are necessary to develop approaches to reliably alter microbiomes to benefit individuals, communities, and societies.
statements.context: The National Microbiome Initiative sought organising principles through comparative research across ecosystems.

completion.title: A fixed mechanistic model predicts and controls an immune response in an independent human cohort.
completion.criterion: For a specified intervention and immune indication, a prospective controlled human study tests a model fixed before access to the validation cohort's outcomes. Changing a defined microbial product or activity must produce the predicted immune effect, meet preregistered prediction-error and immune-effect criteria, and engage the experimentally established host pathway. Achievement is limited to the tested intervention, population, endpoint and conditions. Numerical acceptance limits must come from the study protocol; no common field-wide limits were located.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no published external test combining microbial mechanism, prospective prediction and human immune control was located.
completion.basis: Searches covered NIH microbiome programme goals, FDA development criteria, the Human Microbiome Action causality consensus and the international microbiome-testing consensus. They provided component criteria but no joint completion test or common accuracy, effect-size or duration cutoff. This fallback combines mechanistic intervention and independent human validation for one specified use.

milestones.title: A defined microbial product changes immunity through an experimentally required host pathway.
milestones.criterion: A purified microbial product changes an immune phenotype relative to vehicle, and host-pathway loss-of-function experiments establish pathway dependence. Round and Mazmanian demonstrated this component in mice: Bacteroides fragilis polysaccharide A increased Foxp3-positive regulatory T cells, which restrain immune responses, in wild-type mice but not TLR2-deficient mice. Figure 2A represents three experiments with four mice per group; Figure 2D represents three experiments with at least three mice per group. This establishes a model-specific mechanism, not human prediction.
milestones.set_by: Mechanistic microbiome immunology's purified-product and loss-of-function convention, exemplified by Round and Mazmanian, Figure 2. The published example concerns polysaccharide A and TLR2, not every microbial product.

milestones.title: A microbiome intervention has preclinical safety evidence adequate for initial human testing.
milestones.criterion: The candidate's nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology evidence supports initial human exposure under FDA requirements. The required studies depend on the product and stage of investigation; this is not a universal numerical toxicity cutoff. Evidence of an immune mechanism alone does not satisfy this safety criterion.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Drug Development and Review Definitions, Pre-Clinical Research.
milestones.threshold_quote: data showing that the drug is reasonably safe for use in initial, small-scale clinical studies.

milestones.title: A phase I microbiome study completes 12-month assessment of related grade ≥2 adverse events.
milestones.criterion: NCT02960074 specified assessment of transplant-related adverse events of grade 2 or above over 12 months in 15 adults aged 18–40 years with peanut allergy. The sponsor's registry record gives study completion as 28 July 2021. The subsequent paper reports no safety issues, but its accessible abstract does not provide a grade-by-grade adverse-event table. Completion of this endpoint is distinct from demonstrating efficacy or predicting individual responses.
milestones.set_by: Rima Rachid, Boston Children's Hospital, registered protocol NCT02960074. This endpoint was written for encapsulated faecal microbiota transplantation in peanut allergy; it is not a general phase I duration requirement. Sponsor record accessed through its ICH GCP mirror.
milestones.threshold_quote: Presence of FMT-related adverse events grade 2 or above

milestones.title: Independent clinical studies confirm a microbiome marker of immune-treatment response.
milestones.criterion: Independent clinical studies confirm the response marker in its stated context of use. The Human Microbiome Action consensus identifies independent confirmation as part of biomarker qualification but supplies no universal discrimination or calibration cutoff. Relevant evidence remains context-dependent: Lee and colleagues analysed 165 patients with advanced melanoma plus 147 previously published metagenomic samples and found cohort-dependent associations with immune-checkpoint-inhibitor response. These observational associations do not establish intervention causality.
milestones.set_by: Human Microbiome Action consortium, State of the art and the future of microbiome-based biomarkers, Panel 2.

milestones.title: A controlled human study measures outcomes after microbiome-guided versus standard treatment.
milestones.criterion: An interventional study completes the comparison of microbiome-test-guided modulation with a standard approach and determines their comparative clinical effectiveness. The international consensus recommends this comparison, preferably randomised, without prescribing a universal benefit threshold. This establishes the clinical effect of using the microbiome information; completion additionally requires successful prospective prediction tied to a defined microbial mechanism. The supplied peanut-allergy study used non-randomised, open-label groups and does not establish this comparison.
milestones.set_by: International consensus panel on microbiome testing in clinical practice, Working Group 5; a recommended clinical-utility comparison, with randomisation preferred.
milestones.threshold_quote: interventional studies, preferably with a randomised design, should compare the effectiveness of a targeted modulation of gut microbiome

not_found: No published joint completion standard or common numerical prediction-accuracy threshold was located in the programmes, regulatory criteria and consensus documents searched.
No prospective controlled human study validating the complete mechanistic prediction-and-intervention capability was located.
PubMed returned no usable primary-study text, and the Science journal page returned an access error; the Broad Institute's reproduction of the primary abstract was accessible.
ClinicalTrials.gov supplied no usable study-record text and its API could not be opened; NCT02960074 was readable through an ICH GCP mirror.

results.finding: B. ovatus bile salt hydrolase deletion impaired food-allergy protection in mice; 16 received the mutant.
results.detail: The experiment deleted a microbial enzyme, rather than testing a purified microbial product with host-pathway loss of function.
results.quote:
Deletion of a bile salt hydrolase in a candidate protective
Bacteroides
abrogated FA suppression in mice.

results.finding: Among 15 FMT recipients, 2 had possibly or probably related grade 2 adverse events.
results.detail: The paper reports adverse-event grades but does not establish completion of the 12-month related adverse-event assessment; the 12-month exit visit was optional.
results.quote: Of the 15 participants who underwent FMT, three had grade 1 and two had grade 2 adverse events (AE) that were thought to be possibly or probably related to FMT, all of which resolved within 12 to 48 hours

results.finding: In 15 FMT recipients, B. xylanisolvens abundance was greater in responders at baseline.
results.detail: This targeted association comes from one small clinical cohort; independent confirmation of the proposed response marker is not reported.
results.quote:
Follow-up targeted statistical analysis of
Bacteroides
species in the human MGX dataset showed that
B. xylanisolvens
, exhibited greater abundance at baseline and post-FMT in responders compared to non-responders.

results.finding: In a phase I FMT study, 15 adults with peanut allergy had no reported safety concerns.
results.detail: The research highlight does not report the 12-month assessment or grade-specific, transplant-related adverse events.

results.finding: Purified B. fragilis PSA increased Foxp3+ Tregs in mice: 4 wild-type mice per group, P < 0.01; at least 3 TLR2-deficient mice per group showed no increase.
results.detail: Figure 2A and Figure 2D each represent three independent experiments. PSA was compared with PBS; the TLR2 loss-of-function result establishes pathway dependence in this mouse model.
results.quote:
In contrast to the
Treg expansion seen in WT animals (see Fig. 2 A), we observed no
difference in the percentage of CD4 +Foxp3+ T cells in TLR2 −/−
mice treated with PSA compared with PBS controls (Fig. 2 D).

results.finding: R-5780: a 28-day GLP repeat-dose mouse study found no gastrointestinal adverse findings; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The paper reports that first-in-human testing is underway and that clinical dose selection drew on the repeat-dose toxicology NOAEL and preclinical pharmacology, biodistribution, and clearance data.
results.quote: In the 28-day GLP toxicology studies, no gastrointestinal adverse findings were observed, and histopathological evaluation showed normal mucosal architecture, supporting good local tolerability.

results.finding: In 338 advanced NSCLC patients, fecal A. muciniphila detection was associated with a 10-percentage-point increase in objective response to checkpoint inhibitors.
results.detail: The prospective cohort excluded patients from the authors’ earlier NSCLC analysis. The paper also reports confirmation of Akk enrichment in responders by another group’s 37-patient NSCLC study. The association is observational; the abundance cutoff was derived within the 338-patient cohort.
results.quote:

+
patients when considering all (mostly 2L) 338 NSCLC patients (from 18.2% to 28.2% in ORR,

results.finding: TOPOSCORE was associated with overall survival in a prospective cohort of 77 NSCLC patients; p = 0.0214.
results.detail: This is validation in a separate cohort, but the text does not establish confirmation by an independent study. The authors also state that TOPOSCORE cannot distinguish prognostic from treatment-predictive effects on overall survival.

results.finding: In 121 IBS patients, microbiome-guided diet versus low-FODMAP diet showed no significant difference in symptom-score change (P = 0.29).
results.detail: The randomized study completed a clinical comparison, but did not establish successful prospective prediction of an immune response through a defined microbial mechanism. Differential dropout between groups also limits interpretation.
results.quote:
For the primary outcome, there was a change in IBS-SSS of2112.7 for those in the PD group vs299.9
for those in the FODMAP diet group (P 5 0.29).

results.finding: In 69 adults with IBS assessed at 12 months, the microbiome-guided diet had a 28.0 percentage-point higher symptom response rate than low-FODMAP.
results.detail: The randomized comparison reports clinical effectiveness, but it does not establish successful prospective prediction tied to a defined microbial mechanism or host immune pathway. The 12-month follow-up had substantial attrition and was not prospectively powered for between-group comparisons.
results.quote:
At 12 months,  IBS-SSS responder 
rates were higher with PD than LFD (62.5% vs 34.5%; absolute risk difference +28.0%, 
95% CI 4.2–47.7; Fisher p = 0.029), and IBS-QOL, HADS-anxiety, and HADS-depression 
showed more favourable trajectories with PD.
